Goodbye Durban

By: Jacqui Jayamaha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Durban is marketed as a prime holiday destination but many of its citizens are deeply worried about the unprecedented increase of criminal elements populating the beachfront.

Unique Selling Point:
This will be a disturbing insert looking at a multi billion rand investment verses urban rot that is rapidly setting into Durban’s iconic Beachfront.


Summary:
Façade - Durban’s upmarket hotels and 5 star apartment blocks, situated along South and North beach promenades, have become just an attractive façade along the Golden Mile, which is the City’s major economic hub. The reality is, a tourist’s much anticipated walk along the beach is peppered with constant harassment by beggars, the stench of crack cocaine and the ever present danger of stepping on used heroin syringes strewn along the shore. Children playing in the sand stand the risk of stepping on shards of broken glass from bottles smashed to make crack pipes. Users can sometimes be seen in plain sight shooting up. The iconic souvenir ladies are a cover for dealers that pay them a fee for sitting outside their stalls and the sand sculptor artists sleep under the piers that they use as a shelter, a place to shoot up and a toilet. Full term twin babies thrown next to a trash can greet joggers on a beach front run. And yet the municipality is spending R39 billion to upgrade this area but with no apparent plans to address the criminal element threatening the health and safety of visitors.

Further information:
Surfing is one of Durban’s major international sports attractions and according to seasoned locals, the risk of getting pricked by a needle while running into the waves is increasing.
Senior Life Guard, Quentin Shabalala, says he is always on the alert for discarded syringes and shows us where the sand sculptors live under the pier.

Philip Sithole the Deputy Manager of Durban Economic development will be asked toexpalin where the R39 billion rand budget for the upgrades will be spent as well as the VIP question, what will be done to handle the growing criminal elements populating the beachfront areas.

Colonel Mbele - spokesperson for SAPS will explain what the police are doing to control the criminals on the beachfront, what plans are planned for the future.

Press Release:


Goodbye Durban?
Holidays are approaching with an estimated 2-million holidaymakers descending on Durban’s beaches. But the once beautiful sandy beaches are now littered with heroin needles and shards of broken glass from bottles smashed to make crack pipes. In the midst of this, the City is planning a R39-billion facelift along the coastal promenade. Carte Blanche investigates how Durban’s beachfront precinct could put the health and safety of visitors at risk.
Producer: Jacqui Jayamaha
Presenter: Claire Mawisa
Watch the trailer


Script:


Goodbye Durban - 10mins

V/O: December approaches, and Durban is getting ready for the annual influx of over 2 million holidaymakers that earns it over R 3billion a year. They come for the Golden Mile – a 6km stretch of beachfront from Blue Lagoon Beach in the north to uShaka Marine Park in the south. It’s Durban’s lifeblood – four and five star seafront apartments, hotels and restaurants, a stone’s throw away from the International Convention Centre and Moses Mabida Stadium. But a steady increase in violent stabbings and robberies on the streets around the beach have locals worried.

Int Bandile Sithole “As you can see we are less that 200 meters away from the beach, and we have our restaurant here, our beautiful Egagasini and this is where the crime happens”.

V/O Restaurateur, Bandile Sithole’s family, has invested millions of rands into their high-end beachfront eatery but crime levels are having a negative effect on the business.

Int Sithole “This time in Durban we are facing a lot of problems, we got tourists coming in from all over the world, All over South Africa, coming into Durban. From) hotels they coming to have fun not knowing, we have a terrible problem with drug dealers. It’s been a hectic problem, especially for businesses around here.

Link “The deterioration in this coastal capital has reached epidemic proportions leaving residents, property owners and the private sector feeling fearful and frustrated and unless the authorities begin meaningful rehabilitation of the city –it could be “Goodbye Durban”.

V/O Durban City Council is in the process of managing a R39 billion upgrade in a waterfront development – part one will be complete in the middle of next year.

V/O For local surfer Mike Frew it can’t come soon enough.

Mike “I’ve been surfing in Durban for about 30 years and I’ve never seen the beachfront as bad as it is over the last 2 to 3 years.
There’s actually people living under the pier. They go to the toilet on the beach, it’s washing into the shore break it’s shocking.

V/O The beach has seen a massive influx of homeless and unemployed people seeking the opportunities that come with tourism. Private security estimates that up to 60% of people who hang out here use illegal drugs that are cheap and easy to get. Raz Ali heads up Boss UIP’s safer city project where they work with municipal authorities like the police, Metro and Durban Solid Waste. We followed his undercover informant into the street just a 100 meters behind the hotels.

UPS FROM VIDEO OF DEALING - Sound up from clip “4, give me change! Wait now, what is your problem?” Jussis

V/O Within minutes the informant bought crack cocaine and heroin. In plain sight dealers line the pavements supplying any drugs for cash – and the users scramble for a quick fix.

V/O Ali believes heroin dealing and addiction fuels crime. But it’s not just the drugs that are impacting the beach precinct.

Claire “I see shocking evidence, needles just lying open in the street?”
Ali “Yes these are used syringes possibly, from the heroin users in the area. Now there’s a lot of dealing of heroin in this particular area, this is what’s going on.
Ali “Babies nappies here, tyre used as a toilet etc”
Claire Lots of activity obviously,
Ali Lots of activity, it’s clear that homeless people have been living here.
Claire The smell
Ali Ya
Claire Wow Oh my God!
Ali Used babies’ napkins, a lot of human feces all over the place and inside the tyre, you can see this has been used as a toilet.

Link “Being constantly aware of your surroundings and watching where you walk, is becoming a necessity in the streets that are just behind the hotels and what I saw here was frightening, Given a choice I wouldn’t walk some of these areas never mind just at night but even in broad daylight.”

Int Sithole Kids can’t even go to the beach to play anymore or go and surf anymore, without walking over a needle. Our beaches aren’t safe anymore.

Mike So now what it’s done is that literally every time you come down for a surf ….running down to the water’s edge which is the most anticipated, most exciting part of your surf, you’re super worried about stepping on a needle.

V/O Which is exactly what happened to chiropractor Grant Harper who was taking photos on the beach.

Harper Int “I just happened to be setting up my tripod and I felt a prick looked down…needle….talks about ARVs…other things you got Hepatitis and things like tetanus.

Int woman Most of us, you see when you finished to spike you are high, you don’t care what you are doing you don’t see, you can even leave it here, and just go.

V/O Drug abuse often pushes users into a life of crime.

Int Lady We wanna smoke, we wanna have money but we’re not working so we’ll go outside, we’ll grab somebody’s things for us to get a smoke.

Int Lady We think about the money for skyf, we think about to steal, because we want quick money to support your habit.
Int Handsome “ We smoking drugs near our home, we steal it, we kill the people.

Claire And why Durban, why is everyone here in Durban in this particular area?

Int Handsome Because Durban everything is cheap here, even the whoonga is cheap, the rock is cheap, everything is cheap, that’s why they like to come here. (subtitles)

V/O Even the iconic curio vendors with their vibrant stalls along the beach seem to have become – at least in some cases – a front to sell drugs. (Up sound Zulu and reply lady Zulu) These ladies instructed the undercover informant to come back later to buy his drugs, which is exactly what he did!

V/O Ebrahim Vadachia, UIP Chairman says with police resources stretched to the limit, crime prevention is a luxury – police can only put out fires.

Mr V “There’s not enough governmental and other departmental attention is given to the problem, and that is why you’ll find the rate of decay increasing with each passing day, unless it is arrested by a concerted action on governmental and all levels.
Mr V “It is chasing away a lot of tourism, and I can understand why, I wouldn’t bring, personally, our families into a situation where I know it’s a given that chances are things like this are going to happen.

V/O Deputy City manager of Economic Development and planning, Philip Sithole believes he has the solution. A massive R39 billion investment is planned to upgrade the Beachfront and the adjoining inner city area.

Int P Sithole “It will be the latest in Africa in terms of developing the waterfront.
5.00 Int P Sithole “It’s an investment that is going to create an environment for people who are interested in the tourism space…. and attract investors to Durban, more especially foreign investors.
23.56 Claire Will this massive investment even address elements of criminality?
29.10 Int P Sithole We know the problems that are faced by major cities in South Africa.
30:17 Int P Sithole Now I’m telling you if we have more….. investors coming and investing in the inner city, some of these problems will go away we’ll reduce the level of these problems.

V/O But Bandile Sithole the owner of Egagasini, doesn’t share the city’s optimism that upgrades will address the crime rate.

Int B Sithole First of all it’s a waste, I think if you’re going to spend that much money on the city - I would say we are investing in big crime in Durban!
Our crime will never stop until we stop drug dealing, our crime will never stop.
Claire I was shocked when I arrived and I was walking around and I saw needles on the floor, and hundreds of homeless people under a bridge, tyres being used as a toilet.
Int Philip. What you saw this morning you’ll see it in Cape Town, you’ll see it in Johannesburg, because these are major cities in South Africa, because people they flock into the cities.

V/O Will the multi billion rand upgrade address social degeneration or will it simply attract more criminals?

Mr V ” I hope the powers that be do the right thing”.

Philip Sithole the Deputy Manager of Durban Economic development will be asked toexpalin where the R39 billion rand budget for the upgrades will be spent as well as the VIP question, what will be done to handle the growing criminal elements populating the beachfront areas. Colonel Mbele - spokesperson for SAPS will explain what the police are doing to control the criminals on the beachfront, what plans are planned for the future.
